lead: Disconnect the source and the stored energy does not vanish at once: an inductor's current and a capacitor's voltage fall through the resistance along a smooth exponential. The speed is set by one number, the time constant τ. This source-free (natural) response, with no battery or generator, only L or C and R, explains why a camera-flash capacitor still holds charge after switch-off and why a relay coil's current collapses in milliseconds. The same maths runs sensor circuits, filters and snubbers.
prereq: You need: the V-I relations of L and C from circuit elements and laws, and initial and final conditions for the starting value at t = 0.

sections.h3: The first-order circuit and its equation

blocks.text: Source-free means the independent source is removed or switched out at t = 0. Only the storage element and R remain. In an RL circuit, an inductor L with initial current I₀ is connected across a resistor R. KVL gives v<sub>L</sub> + v<sub>R</sub> = 0. Use v<sub>L</sub> = L di/dt and v<sub>R</sub> = R i:
L di/dt + R i = 0  ⇒  di/dt = −(R/L) i
blocks.where: L is inductance in henry (H); R is resistance in ohm (Ω); i is the loop current in ampere (A) at time t in second (s).

blocks.text: The solution is i(t) = I₀ e<sup>−t/τ</sup> with τ = L/R. I₀ is the current at t = 0 in A. For an RC circuit, a capacitor C charged to V₀ is connected across R. KCL at the node gives C dv/dt + v/R = 0, so RC dv/dt + v = 0. The voltage is v(t) = V₀ e<sup>−t/τ</sup> with τ = RC. V₀ is the capacitor voltage at t = 0 in V. Both are first-order because one storage element sets the answer, and the final value is zero. When several resistors remain, R is the equivalent resistance R<sub>eq</sub> seen from the terminals of L or C. Some syllabi call this the natural response or free response.

sections.h3: The time constant and the tangent

blocks.text: τ is the time constant, measured in seconds. At t = τ, e<sup>−1</sup> = 0.368. The current or voltage has fallen to 36.8 % of its starting value. After 2τ it is 13.5 %, after 3τ 5.0 %, and after 5τ 0.67 %. The 5τ rule says the transient is practically zero; it is not exactly zero. The half-life is τ ln 2 ≈ 0.693τ.

Differentiate x(t) = x(0)e<sup>−t/τ</sup> at t = 0: slope = −x(0)/τ. The tangent line is x = x(0) − [x(0)/τ]t. It meets zero at t = τ. That is the geometric meaning of τ: follow the starting slope and you reach zero one time constant later.

R changes the two circuits in opposite ways. For RL, τ = L/R: a larger R gives a smaller τ, because the same current through a larger resistor burns the stored ½LI₀² faster (power i²R). For RC, τ = RC: a larger R gives a larger τ, because the capacitor can push only a smaller current v/R through it. This is a favourite comparison question.

Stored energy is ½ L I₀² in the inductor and ½ C V₀² in the capacitor. The resistor has no storage; it turns that energy into heat. In RL, p<sub>R</sub> = i²R = I₀²R e<sup>−2t/τ</sup>. Integrate from 0 to ∞: total = I₀²R (τ/2) = ½ L I₀². In RC, p<sub>R</sub> = v²/R = (V₀²/R) e<sup>−2t/τ</sup>. Total = (V₀²/R)(RC/2) = ½ C V₀². All the initial stored energy ends in R as t → ∞. At t = τ, the fraction burnt is 1 − e<sup>−2</sup> = 0.865, so 86.5 % is gone and 13.5 % remains. This energy view explains why a relay coil needs a diode: the inductor's ½LI² must go somewhere when the switch opens.

figure.caption: The worked example: the coil current falls from 2 A as 2e⁻²⁰⁰ᵗ A. The tangent at t = 0 hits zero at t = τ = 5 ms, where the curve itself is at 36.8 % of 2 A; the current reaches 0.2 A at 11.5 ms.

examples.question: An inductor L = 0.5 H carries a steady current I₀ = 2 A. At t = 0 it is connected across a resistor R = 100 Ω. Find τ, i(t), and the time to reach 0.2 A.
steps: This is a source-free RL circuit. The time constant is τ = L/R.
The current decay is i(t) = I₀ e<sup>−t/τ</sup> = 2 e<sup>−t/0.005</sup> = 2 e<sup>−200t</sup> A. Here 200 s⁻¹ = 1/τ.
Set i(t) = 0.2 A: 0.2 = 2 e<sup>−200t</sup>. Divide by 2: 0.1 = e<sup>−200t</sup>.
Take natural logarithms: ln 0.1 = −200t. So t = −ln 0.1 ÷ 200 = ln 10 ÷ 200.
examples.answer: τ = 0.005 s = 5 ms; i(t) = 2e<sup>−200t</sup> A; the current is 0.2 A at t = 11.5 ms.
examples.check:
import math
L = 0.5
R = 100.0
I0 = 2.0
tau = L / R
k = R / L
t = tau * math.log(10)
print(tau)
print(k)
print(t)

examples.question: A 50 μF capacitor has been charged to 24 V. At t = 0 it is switched across a 6 kΩ and a 3 kΩ resistor in parallel. Find τ, v(t), the current in the 6 kΩ resistor at t = 50 ms, and the energy each resistor absorbs in the end.
steps: Equivalent resistance seen by C: R<sub>eq</sub> = (6 × 3)/(6 + 3) = 2 kΩ.

Both resistors see the same voltage, so their powers v²/R are in the ratio 1/6 : 1/3 = 1 : 2. The 6 kΩ resistor absorbs 14.4/3 = 4.8 mJ and the 3 kΩ resistor 9.6 mJ; together 14.4 mJ, all the stored energy.
examples.answer: τ = 0.1 s, v(t) = 24e<sup>−10t</sup> V, 2.43 mA in the 6 kΩ resistor at 50 ms, and 4.8 mJ and 9.6 mJ absorbed by the 6 kΩ and 3 kΩ resistors.
examples.check:
import math
Req=6e3*3e3/9e3; tau=Req*50e-6; v=24*math.exp(-0.05/tau)
print(tau, v, v/6e3*1e3, 0.5*50e-6*24**2*1e3)

traps: Writing τ = R/L for an RL circuit or τ = 1/(RC) for an RC circuit. Check units: τ must come out in seconds.
Writing 63.2 % at t = τ for a decay. A source-free decay has 36.8 % of its starting value left at t = τ; 63.2 % of the final value belongs to a charging curve.
Treating 5τ as exactly zero. About 0.67 % is left, so an exam may ask for the exact expression.
Forgetting that I₀ or V₀ comes from the instant before switching. The inductor current and capacitor voltage cannot jump; see initial and final conditions.
Saying a large R always slows decay. In RL, τ = L/R falls as R rises; in RC, τ = RC rises as R rises.

quiz.q: Define the time constant of a source-free RC circuit and give its unit.
quiz.a: τ = RC; unit second. It is the time for voltage to fall to 1/e ≈ 36.8 % of its initial value.

quiz.q: Write the source-free RL current decay law and define each symbol.
quiz.a: i(t) = I₀e<sup>−t/τ</sup>, τ = L/R. i(t) is current at time t in A; I₀ is initial current in A; L is inductance in H; R is resistance in Ω; τ is in s.

quiz.q: Why does increasing R make an RL current decay faster but an RC voltage decay slower?
quiz.a: RL: τ = L/R, so larger R gives smaller τ. RC: τ = RC, so larger R gives larger τ. Physically, in RL the same current through a larger R dissipates the stored energy faster, while in RC a larger R lets the capacitor push only a smaller current.

quiz.q: An RC circuit has R = 47 kΩ, C = 10 μF, and V₀ = 12 V. Find τ and v(0.1 s).
A source-free RL circuit has L = 2 H, R = 50 Ω, I₀ = 4 A. Find τ and the time to reach 0.5 A.
A charged 1 mF capacitor at 20 V is connected across 2 kΩ at t = 0. Find the initial stored energy and the resistor power at t = 0.
The tangent to a source-free decay at t = 0 cuts the time axis at 8 ms. (a) What is τ? (b) What fraction remains at t = 8 ms? (c) At what time is 1 % left?
quiz.a: (a) The tangent cuts at τ, so τ = 8 ms. (b) e<sup>−1</sup> = 0.368, so 36.8 % remains. (c) e<sup>−t/τ</sup> = 0.01 → t = τ ln 100 = 8 × 4.605 = 36.8 ms.

beyond: Not for the exam. The time constant appears in sensor datasheets as response time, in relay circuits as the L/R decay that a flyback diode must carry, and in battery models as a parallel RC branch. Control engineers quote a 10–90 % rise time of about 2.2τ for a first-order step. Search for RC time constant, RL decay and inductive kickback protection.
